newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Coffee strengthens, wheat and oil look firm.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Coffee strengthens, wheat and oil look firm.

text.p: World coffee prices strengthened still further on Friday, continuing their week's climb, as falling stocks and concerns over strikes in Brazil and Colombia persisted.
July futures for the arabica type of coffee soared almost six percent in the week in New York, reaching 193.50 cents a pound on Friday versus 172 cents last Friday.

Other commodity markets saw wheat looking stronger, on fears that freezing weather in the U.S. Great Plains may have damaged crops, while oil steadied also on the back of the late cold snap in the United States.

The New York Coffee, Sugar and Cocoa Exchange coffee warehouses stocks fell to 67,578 bags on April 16, down from 80,078 bags after a 12,500 bag fall in Mexican coffee stocks in the New Orleans warehouse.
News of a smaller-than-expected rise in U.S. March green coffee stocks earlier in the week was also seen supporting the market.
Near-term supply concerns were further intensified by a proposed national strike in the ports of Brazil, the world's number one coffee producer, even though the call met a mixed response.
But a planned truck drivers' strike in Colombia, the second largest coffee producer, was still due to go ahead from Sunday and provided another point of focus for the market.
May coffee futures for premium arabica types leaped to a new life-of-contract high in early Friday trading in New York, notching up a gain of 8.20 cents to trade at 218.00 cents a pound.
May robusta coffee futures in London were also looking firmer, helped up by gains in New York to reach $1,640 per tonne in London's Friday afternoon.
In the grain markets, wheat recovered from midweek lows, but traders said it was still looking volatile having initially surged ahead early in the week after freezing U.S. weekend weather conditions.

Spain saw some rain on Thursday after months of dry weather, but grain prices there remained high on Friday as dealers said the rainfall had not yet been sufficient. Elsewhere in northwest Europe dry weather conditions persisted.

Chicago Board of Trade wheat reached higher in the midsession in Chicago as the extent of last weekend's crop damage in the U.S. Great Plains hard red winter wheat region was not yet clear and uncertainty continued to boost prices.
Traders said a European Union decision on Thursday to halt its weekly export tender for wheat also sparked concern.
"There are all kind of horror stories and they pulled some rain out of Europe. All of a sudden we've gone from bearish to bullish in a week," said Steve Bruce of E.D. and F. Man International.

Low temperatures in the northeastern United States, the world's key heating fuel market, boosted heating oil demand and weather forecasts predict below average temperatures may persist into next week.

"Most people were assuming the heating oil season had run its course and although there's no danger of any supply disruption the U.S. market is looking a little tight on heating oil," one London trader said.
Crude oil prices for benchmark North Sea Brent Blend took a knock earlier in the week when American Petroleum Institute data showed rising U.S. stocks and weak gasoline demand.
In London's Friday afternoon the July Brent futures contract was approaching the $18 a barrel level, but was off the day's high of $18.13.
Copper was looking firmer towards the end of the day in London, helped slightly by a strike which started on Friday at the Escondida mine, the world's biggest copper mine, in Chile.
Gold in London ended the day little changed, still stuck in a range of $340-$345.
